answer.label: Not Bruce Lee — it’s the Hsin Hsin Ming of Sengcan
answer.authorName: Jianzhi Sengcan (Third Zen Patriarch); English by Arthur Waley
answer.authorDates: Sengcan: d. 606 CE · Third Patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism
answer.sourceLine: These are the opening lines of the ‘Hsin Hsin Ming’ (‘On Trust in the Heart’), a 6th-century Chan Buddhist poem attributed to Sengcan. The exact English wording is Arthur Waley’s translation ↗, published in Edward Conze’s Buddhist Texts Through the Ages (1954). Bruce Lee copied it into his notebooks, and it later appeared in his posthumously published works — but he neither wrote nor originated it.

source.excerpt:
The Perfect Way is only difficult for those who pick and choose;
Do not like, do not dislike; all will then be clear.
Make a hairbreadth difference, and Heaven and Earth are set apart;
If you want the truth to stand clear before you, never be for or against.
The struggle between ‘for’ and ‘against’ is the mind’s worst disease;
While the deep meaning is misunderstood, it is useless to meditate on Rest.
trail: Wikiquote lists this passage on its Bruce Lee page under “Misattributed” ↗, noting it is actually from the Xinxin Ming of Sengcan.
The Wikiquote entry for Sengcan ↗ gives the identical wording as Arthur Waley’s translation, from Conze’s Buddhist Texts Through the Ages (1954).
The Terebess Asia Online archive ↗ reproduces Waley’s full translation with the citation “Buddhist Texts Through the Ages, Edward Conze (ed.), 1954, pp. 296–298.”
Wikiquote notes the wording also appears in Huston Smith’s The Religions of Man (1958), the popular route by which the Waley rendering reached mid-century readers such as Lee.
source.excerptNote: The opening of the poem in Arthur Waley’s translation. The lines circulated under Bruce Lee’s name are this passage, lightly re-punctuated into prose.

source.rightsNote: The 6th-century Chinese original is long in the public domain, but the specific English wording quoted here is Arthur Waley’s translation, first published in 1954 — well after the 1931 U.S. cutoff — and is therefore still in copyright. Public-domain status attaches only to the ancient original, not to this modern rendering.

author.name: Jianzhi Sengcan
author.heading: Who really wrote it
author.metaLine: d. 606 CE · Third Patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism
author.bio: Jianzhi Sengcan (Chien-chih Seng-ts’an) is traditionally honored as the Third Patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China, successor to Huike. He is credited by tradition with the Hsin Hsin Ming, one of the earliest and most beloved Zen poems, whose theme is the mind at peace once it stops grasping at like and dislike. The attribution is traditional rather than documentary — and the English words that made the poem famous in the West are those of its 20th-century translator, Arthur Waley.

misattribution.heading: How Bruce Lee got the credit
misattribution.intro: Bruce Lee is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for borrowed wisdom. This passage is a genuine, cited quotation — but it is a Zen poem Lee admired and transcribed, not something he authored.

items.why: Lee copied these lines into his personal notes, and they were printed in his posthumously assembled books such as Tao of Jeet Kune Do (1975). Readers took the words as his own. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are the opening of the Hsin Hsin Ming of Sengcan ↗, in Arthur Waley’s 1954 translation ↗ — roughly fourteen centuries before Bruce Lee.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The Hsin Hsin Ming makes one austere point: the ‘Perfect Way’ is not hard because it is hidden, but because the mind cannot stop preferring — sorting every experience into liked and disliked, for and against. Drop that habit, the poem says, and clarity is already here.

That message dovetailed neatly with Bruce Lee’s own philosophy of fluidity and non-attachment, which is why he transcribed it — and why, once his notebooks were published, the lines were so easily mistaken for his.
